note: Fushimi Inari's daily life (issue #357): the people to know, their hours, the jobs, the counters and the calendar. Built into web/data/fushimi-inari/life.json by pipeline/life.py, which resolves every place. Facts in 'fact' are checked against the sources in docs/cities/fushimi-inari.md and docs/cities/kyoto-sights.md (section 3, which also gives the Okusha's coordinates); each event carries its own source.

bonds.title: The shrine attendant

places.where: The Romon gate, seeing the groups through

bonds.busy: ようお参り. I'm on duty at the hall just now. I'm at the foot of the approach in the mornings and through the day.

ranks.title: Rice
ranks.invite: You bowed at the torii. Not everyone does. Have you a little of the {slot}? I'll tell you whose house this is.
talk: The shrine dates itself to 711, when a man of the Hata clan enshrined the kami on the three peaks. That is before Kyoto was a city at all.
Inari is the kami of rice. In the Edo period rice was money, so Inari became the kami of money too. The merchants worked that out quickly.
ranks.fact: Fushimi Inari Taisha dates its founding to 711, when Hata no Irogu enshrined the kami on the three peaks of Inari-yama.

ask.q: So who do you think pays for all the torii?

options.reply: Right. A wish made or a wish granted, and a gate goes up with the name on the back. It has been done since the Edo period.
We only stand them up. Each one is given, by a business or a family, with the name on the back.

request.text: Walk up to where the Senbon Torii begin
request.ask: Have you been up to the two tunnels yet? Read the back of a gate on the way down.

ranks.title: The jewel and the key
talk: You read one. A company's name and a date, always on the side you see coming down.
The foxes are not the kami. They are the messengers. Look at their mouths: a jewel for the kami's spirit, a key for the rice store, an ear of rice, a scroll.
And the gate they guard was given by Hideyoshi in 1589, when his mother fell ill and recovered.
ranks.fact: The Romon of Fushimi Inari was given by Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1589 in thanks for his mother's recovery; the foxes beside it hold a jewel and the key to the rice store.

gives.name: An attendant's directions
gives.text: Bearings: you know the mountain's paths

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Try your eye on the Romon: press G and guess its height. Most people say twenty metres.

ranks.title: Heavy or light
talk: Fourteen metres or so, yes. Tall, for a shrine gate.
At the Okusha, past the tunnels, there are two stone lanterns. Make a wish, then lift the stone off the top. If it's lighter than you feared, the wish will come true.
I'm not permitted to say how heavy they are. I can say everyone makes the same face. The office has votive boards to go up there, if you'd carry them: it's paid.
ranks.fact: At the Okusha behind the Senbon Torii stand the omokaru-ishi: lift the stone from a lantern after a wish, and if it feels lighter than expected the wish is said to come true.

ask.q: And what do you do if it's heavy?

options.text: Lift it anyway, and work harder
options.reply: That is the correct theology. I'll put in a word with the foxes.

gives.name: The office's runner
gives.text: A paid errand for the shrine office, in your diary under Work

request.text: Carry the votive boards up to the Okusha
request.ask: The boards are tied and waiting. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: Open all night
talk: They arrived dry and in order. Thank you.
People ask when we close. We don't. The gates have no doors to shut: the mountain is open all night, every night, and the lanterns stay lit.
At two in the morning it's the cats, a runner or two, and the sound of the stream. I did nights for a year. I recommend it.
ranks.fact: The grounds and mountain paths of Fushimi Inari Taisha are open 24 hours a day, every day, without an entrance fee.

request.text: Walk the Senbon Torii at night
request.ask: Go through the tunnels once after dark, when the lanterns are the only light. Then come and tell me.

ranks.title: Thirty thousand
talk: You went up in the dark. Then you've seen it as we do.
There are about thirty thousand Inari shrines in Japan: on department-store roofs, in factory yards, at the ends of alleys. Every one is a branch of this mountain.
So when you pass a little red gate anywhere in the country, you'll know where it leads. ようお参り.
ranks.fact: Fushimi Inari Taisha is the head shrine of some 30,000 Inari shrines across Japan.

gives.name: A word from the shrine office
gives.text: 15% more for every job at Fushimi Inari

bonds.title: The inari sushi shop
bonds.where: At the entrance of the Senbon Torii
bonds.busy: Not now, I've a queue out of the door. Come by in the daytime when it eases, or towards evening before I shut.

ranks.title: Fox ears
ranks.invite: You're the first today to keep right without being told. Have you a bit of the {slot}? Sit down, I'll explain your lunch.
talk: Inari-zushi here is a triangle. Fox ears. In Tokyo they make it a little barrel, a rice bale. Same thing, different animal.
The tofu is simmered sweet with soy, and in Kyoto we put hemp seeds in the rice, for the crunch. My mother-in-law counted them out. I don't.
ranks.fact: Inari sushi in Kansai is folded into a triangle, like a fox's ear; in Kanto it is shaped like a bale of rice.

ask.q: And what goes on kitsune udon, do you think?

options.reply: The same. Kitsune means fox. In this neighbourhood, everything a fox likes ends up on a menu.
Heavens, no. Fried tofu. The fox is who likes it, not what's in it.

request.text: Eat something at a counter on the mountain
request.ask: Well? Have you had any yet? I can't talk tofu with someone who hasn't eaten.

ranks.title: Sparrows
talk: Good. Now you've an opinion.
The other thing sold on this approach is grilled sparrow. Sparrows eat the rice, Inari guards the rice, so we eat the sparrows. It has a certain logic.
Fewer shops do it every year, and it's mostly quail now. Now: the tea house at Yotsutsuji wants its sushi carried up. It pays, and you've the legs for it.
ranks.fact: Grilled sparrow, and now more often quail, is a traditional food of the approach to Fushimi Inari: the birds eat the rice that Inari protects.

gives.name: Mrs. Ota's carrier
gives.text: A paid delivery up the mountain, in your diary under Work

request.text: Carry the inari sushi up to Yotsutsuji
request.ask: The boxes are wrapped and waiting. It's in your diary, under Work. Keep them flat.

ranks.title: The fortune in the fold
talk: Up to Yotsutsuji with the rice still warm. You'll do.
Here's one for you. The fortune cookie that Americans think is Chinese: bakers by this shrine still make the older kind, with the paper tucked in the fold. Tsujiura senbei.
Miso and sesame in the batter. They taste of nothing you'd call a biscuit.
ranks.fact: Tsujiura senbei, folded crackers with a paper fortune tucked into the fold, are still baked near Fushimi Inari and are an ancestor of the American fortune cookie.

ask.q: Where would you have guessed they came from?

options.reply: Polite, and right. Japanese bakers took them to California, and the rest is other people's history.
So does everyone. Japanese bakers took them to California about a hundred years ago.

request.text: Buy a small torii or an ema at the shrine office
request.ask: Have you left anything at the shrine yet? The office by the gate has little torii. Everyone leaves one.

ranks.title: Names on the back
talk: A little one. Good. The big ones cost more than my shop makes in a month.
The wood is cedar and the red is lead paint. It lasts some years in this damp, then rots at the foot, and the family pays again or the place goes to the next name.
So the mountain is never finished. There's always a carpenter somewhere on it.
ranks.fact: The torii of Inari-yama, about 10,000 in all, are cedar coated in vermilion red-lead paint; the donor's name and the date are written on the back.

gives.name: Mrs. Ota's regular
gives.text: 20% more for every job at Fushimi Inari

request.text: Walk through the Senbon Torii and read a name
request.ask: Go through the tunnels again and read one name properly, on the way down. Then tell me whose it was.

ranks.title: Keep right
talk: Whose name did you read? No, don't tell me. Somebody's hope, anyway.
All these years I've told people 'up on the right, down on the left'. I used to think I sold sushi. Mostly I direct traffic.
You keep right without being told. Come and eat whenever you like.
ranks.fact: The Senbon Torii are two parallel tunnels of gates behind the main hall, each walked one way: up on the right, down on the left.

bonds.title: The hiker at Yotsutsuji

places.where: The Senbon Torii, setting off up the mountain

bonds.busy: Can't stop, I'll seize up. I'm on the bench at Yotsutsuji in the mornings and through the day, when it's dry.

ranks.title: Halfway
ranks.invite: You've still got breath to talk. Impressive. Got some of the {slot}? Sit. Everyone sits here.
talk: Yotsutsuji: the four-way crossing. It's about halfway by distance and most of the way by effort. From here the path makes a loop round the three peaks.
The top is 233 metres. There's no view up there at all, just altars and trees. The view is here. Nobody tells you that at the bottom.
ranks.fact: Inari-yama is 233 m high; the open view over Kyoto is at Yotsutsuji, partway up, not at the summit.

options.reply: Exactly. You go round, you nod at the top altar, you come back here for the view. That's the whole trick.
Of what? Trees. You go for having been. The picture's here.

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Come up once when the sun's low over the city and take one picture. Then show me.

ranks.title: The western bench
talk: There. The whole basin gone gold, and the sun going down behind the western hills.
This bench faces west and a little north. You get the sunset all year, and after dark the city's a tray of lights with the torii lamps behind you.
Give me your camera a second. There: now it'll keep the lanterns warm and the woods dark, the way your eyes do.
ranks.fact: Yotsutsuji looks west and north-west over the Kyoto basin, so the sun sets beyond the city from its benches.

gives.name: Night on the mountain
gives.text: Photographs after sunset keep the lanterns warm and the woods dark

request.ask: There's a photo list in your diary, under Work. A friend of mine prints a walking map. Do it properly.

ranks.title: Ten thousand altars
talk: Good frames. He'll use them.
Look at the little stone altars beside the path on the way round. Otsuka. Families and guilds set them up, each carved with its own name for the kami. Something like ten thousand on this mountain.
Each has small torii stacked against it like firewood. That's where the little gates from the office end up.
ranks.fact: Inari-yama is covered with otsuka, stone altars set up by worshippers and each carved with their own name for the kami: about 10,000 stand along its paths.

gives.name: A hiker's sky
gives.text: The diary shows the next day hour by hour, and Daichi writes when rain is coming
gives.tip: The steps get slippery: the lower shrines, then.

ask.q: Why would each family want its own?

options.text: A kami with their own name on it
options.reply: That's it. Not the shrine's Inari: theirs. It's the most personal mountain I know.
A bit, maybe. Mostly it's wanting an Inari of your own, with your own name for it.

request.ask: Walk a bit more of it first. When you can find your way down without the signs, come back up.

ranks.title: The fox at the bellows
talk: You've been about. I can tell by the calves.

Round the far side there's a shrine built against a boulder, Mitsurugi-sha. The story is that a swordsmith forged a great blade there with a fox working the bellows. There's a Noh play about it, Kokaji.
Further on is a waterfall where people stand under the cold water to pray. In January. I've watched. From a distance.
ranks.fact: Mitsurugi-sha on Inari-yama stands against a sacred boulder and is tied to the Noh play Kokaji, in which the smith Munechika forges a blade with the help of Inari's fox.

gives.name: The loop
gives.text: Bearings: you know the far side of the mountain

request.text: See the city's lights from Yotsutsuji at night
request.ask: Come up once after dark. The path's lit all the way. Sit on my bench; I shan't be on it.

ranks.title: A tray of lights
talk: So you've seen it lit. Worth the knees?
My company moved me to Osaka and back, twice. The mountain didn't move. Four kilometres round, a couple of hours, most weeks since.
You know the way now. I'm the one on the bench. Bring tea.
ranks.fact: The pilgrims' loop from the main shrine round the three peaks of Inari-yama is about 4 km and takes around two hours.

gives.name: The western bench
gives.text: Light, from a man who waits for sunsets

jobs.title: Which way from Yotsutsuji?
jobs.blurb: Walkers at the crossing ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.done: They thank you, and choose the way down.

jobs.title: Three sights of the mountain
jobs.blurb: A walking map wants the Romon, the Senbon Torii and the crossing at Yotsutsuji. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: "These go on the cover," says the map-maker.

jobs.title: Inari sushi for Yotsutsuji
jobs.blurb: From Mrs. Ota's shop up the mountain path to the tea house at Yotsutsuji, while the rice is warm.
jobs.text: Three flat boxes of inari sushi in a cloth. Up on the right, and keep them level.
jobs.done: The tea house counts the boxes and pours you a tea.

jobs.title: Votive boards for the Okusha
jobs.blurb: From the foot of the approach, through the Romon and the Senbon Torii, to the prayer hall at their far end.
jobs.at_name: Kenta, at the foot of the approach
jobs.text: A bundle of blank fox-faced boards on a cord. They clack as you climb.
jobs.done: The attendant at the Okusha hangs them straight up.

shops.name: Mrs. Ota's counter いなり寿司
shops.where: At the entrance of the Senbon Torii

menu.name: Inari sushi
menu.text: Three triangles of sweet fried tofu packed with vinegared rice, hemp seeds and a little sesame. The shape is a fox's ear.

menu.name: Kitsune udon
menu.text: Thick wheat noodles in a pale Kansai broth, with a square of sweet fried tofu laid on top. Fox noodles: named for who is said to love the tofu.

shops.name: Shrine office 授与所
shops.hello: ようお参り. Take your time.

menu.name: A small torii
menu.text: A vermilion gate the height of your hand. You write a wish and your name on it; one stays on the mountain, and this one goes home with you.

menu.name: A fox ema
menu.text: A white wooden fox's face with no features. You draw them on yourself: no two on the racks look alike, and some are frankly alarming.

shops.name: Tea house at Yotsutsuji 茶屋
shops.hello: You made it. Sit on the bench, the view is free.

menu.name: Hiyashi ame
menu.text: Malt syrup and ginger in cold water: Kansai's summer drink, hardly known in Tokyo. In winter the same thing comes hot and is called ame-yu.

menu.name: Amazake
menu.text: Warm, cloudy and sweet, made from rice and koji. It tastes better at 160 metres than it does at the bottom.

events.title: Hatsumode at Fushimi Inari
events.verb: Join the queue for the first visit of the year
events.text: The first shrine visit of the year. About 2.5 million people come here in the first three days, the most of any shrine in the Kansai region.
lines: The approach is one slow river of coats from the station to the Romon. Police with loudhailers hold the crowd in blocks.
About two and a half million people come in the first three days, most of them to ask for a good year in business. Stalls sell new fortunes and take back last year's.

events.title: Hatsuuma Taisai
events.text: The first day of the horse in February, the day the kami is said to have come down on the mountain in 711. It fell on 1 February in 2026.
lines: The first horse day of February: by tradition the day Inari came down on the three peaks, in 711. The shrine counts this as its birthday.
People take home a sprig of cedar from the mountain with a paper streamer tied to it, the shirushi no sugi, for the household shelf.

events.title: Inari-sai: the mikoshi come home
events.text: On 3 May the shrine's five mikoshi return from their resting place in the town, ending the Inari festival, the shrine's greatest.
lines: Five mikoshi come back up the approach on 3 May, after about two weeks at their resting place near Kyoto Station.
The parish is not here on the mountain but in the streets round and south of Kyoto Station. Once a year the kami go to their people, and today they come home.

events.title: Taue-sai: the rice planting
events.verb: Follow the planters to the sacred paddy
events.text: On 10 June, seedlings for the rice offered to the kami are planted in the shrine's own paddy, to a dance performed beside it.
lines: Women in sedge hats step into the shrine's small paddy and plant the seedlings in rows, while shrine maidens dance the rice-planting dance, the Ota-mai, on the bank.
The rice is cut again in October and offered here in November. It is the reason for everything else on this mountain.

events.title: Motomiya-sai: the lantern eve
events.text: In late July, worshippers from Inari shrines all over Japan come back to the head shrine. On the eve, every stone lantern and thousands of red paper ones are lit from 18:00.
lines: Every stone lantern on the mountain is lit by hand, and red paper lanterns hang in rows along the approach and the torii. The shrine calls it the rite of ten thousand lamps.
It falls on the Sunday or holiday after the midsummer dog days begin: in 2026, the eve on 19 July and the festival on the 20th.

events.title: Hitaki-sai: the fire festival
events.text: On 8 November, after the harvest, prayer sticks sent from all over Japan are burned in three great fires in thanks to the kami of rice.
lines: Three fire beds, lit with rice straw. Priests feed them with wooden prayer sticks by the armful, more than a hundred thousand in an afternoon.
Each stick carries a name and a wish. The smoke goes up past the torii, and the year's rice has been thanked for.
